analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set safe nurse staffing plans, with direct-care nurses holding the majority on the committee that writes them.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee in the 112th Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a vote, despite a bipartisan lead sponsor team and 21 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that takes Medicare patients to adopt a hospital-wide plan for how many registered nurses must be on each unit and each shift, with a committee made up of at least 55% direct-care nurses deciding those levels. Hospitals would have to post daily nurse counts for the public, submit staffing data to the government for publication on Hospital Compare, and face civil fines for violations. It also protects nurses who refuse an unsafe assignment from being fired or punished, and bans retaliation against patients and employees who file complaints.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who get safer staffing shown to reduce falls, infections, medication errors, and deaths, and registered nurses, who gain a say in staffing decisions, protection from retaliation, and the right to refuse assignments outside their training or that violate the staffing plan.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each Medicare-participating hospital to implement a hospital-wide nurse staffing plan that sets an appropriate number of registered nurses for each unit and each shift, based on patient numbers and intensity of care.

Creates a hospital nurse staffing committee in which at least 55% of members must be direct-care registered nurses (not managers or administrators), giving bedside nurses a majority voice in staffing decisions.

Requires hospitals to post daily, in a visible place, the number of licensed and unlicensed nursing staff on each unit, and to make the staffing plan and evaluations available to the public; the Secretary must publish submitted staffing data on the Hospital Compare website.

Lets a nurse refuse an assignment that violates the staffing plan or that she or he is not trained for without compromising patient safety, and bans discrimination or retaliation against patients or employees who complain, with court remedies including reinstatement and lost wages for nurses and $5,000 in liquidated damages for patients.
Allows civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with higher penalties for hospitals with a pattern of violations, and public notice of penalized hospitals.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare-participating hospitals, which must hire and schedule enough registered nurses to meet the plans their staffing committees approve, absorb penalties, and run new data-collection and public-reporting systems, with no new federal payment attached.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals would bear the cost of additional registered nurses without new federal reimbursement, a burden that weighs hardest on rural hospitals (which get four years instead of two to comply) and hospitals already operating on thin margins.

The bill sets no fixed nurse-to-patient ratio; each hospital's committee writes its own adjustable minimums, so actual staffing would depend heavily on how seriously each hospital's committee (management-influenced) interprets the requirements.

Enforcement is modest: civil money penalties start at no more than $10,000 per knowing violation, and hospitals that violate only the data-reporting rules instead lose Medicare payment for that data, a lighter-touch remedy than losing Medicare participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — fewer falls, infections, medication errors, and avoidable deaths tied to understaffing — goes to patients and is supported by the research cited in the bill's own findings, and nurses gain real workplace protections. The main cost is hospital labor expense without new federal funding, which is exactly why the bill drew hospital-sector resistance and never advanced. The flexible committee design softens the burden but also weakens the guarantee, so the bill is a genuine improvement for patients more than airtight protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees and then to their Health subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the bill on March 2, 2011, joined by Rep. Steven LaTourette, a Republican, as a lead cosponsor — a bipartisan sponsorship team.

The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee, a dual referral that splits jurisdiction and gives each committee only partial responsibility.
Within two weeks it was referred to the Health subcommittees of both committees, the level where most bills go no further.

The action history records no hearing, no committee vote, no report, and no floor action after the subcommittee referrals; the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress without ever coming to a vote.

The bill would have taken effect through Medicare's conditions of participation: hospitals that failed to meet the staffing requirements would have faced civil money penalties and corrective action plans rather than direct loss of Medicare payment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare hospitals are better off because the bill died: they avoided a requirement to fund larger nurse staffing levels, publish daily staffing counts, and pay penalties for violations, while patients and nurses got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare hospitals, which avoided staffing mandates

for.name: Lois Capps
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Registered Nurse Safe Staffing Act of 2011 on March 2, 2011.

for.name: Steven LaTourette
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as the lead Republican original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: 21 House cosponsors (20 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing but only a small fraction of the chamber.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and referred it to its Health subcommittee, where it received no hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (holds Medicare payment jurisdiction)
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral and sent it to its Health subcommittee, taking no further action on the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and committee leadership in the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Under House rules, committee action on the bill never occurred, and the bill never received floor time in a chamber led by the opposing party.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed federally mandated nurse staffing ratios and reporting requirements, which carry significant labor costs without new reimbursement; no industry lobbying appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat (Capps) with a Republican (LaTourette) leading, and 21 cosponsors split 20-1 toward Democrats — but the bill died quietly in committee, so no vote reveals how the chamber would have split.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to fund more registered-nurse hours per shift, post daily staffing counts publicly, submit staffing data for federal publication, and pay up to $10,000-plus per knowing violation — all costs with no new federal reimbursement. The bill's benefit to patients comes directly at hospitals' expense, which is why hospital-sector resistance to mandated staffing is consistent and well documented even though the record here shows only the bill's quiet death.

Nurses would have gained a 55% majority on the committees that write staffing plans, the right to refuse unsafe or untrained assignments, whistleblower protection with court-enforceable remedies, and staffing levels tied to reducing burnout and turnover — the bill's findings note 25% of nurses considering leaving direct care over staffing.

The bill allows hospitals to hire third-party entities with demonstrated expertise to collect and submit nursing quality data, creating work for health-data firms, though hospitals bear the compliance obligation either way.
